utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On Wednesday, 4th of April, I would like to greet the representatives of the OTP, the Defence counsel, the accused, and the witness, the Ambassador. I don't want to forget everybody else who is helping us with our task. The cross-examination is about to proceed. I understand that Mr. Karnavas needs about three more hours, more or less, for his cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have received some time from the other teams. I believe I have three hours plus 20 minutes in total. Hopefully some may be generous to give me some time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I trust you had a wonderful evening yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off while we were speaking about Cutileiro, so I'm going to continue with that until we finish and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. The screen where the printing comes up is blank for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Good enough. All right. And let's pick up where we left off, the Cutileiro Plan. Now, I want to show you or share with you a document, 1D 00525. This is a letter dated April 26, 1992. And you have the translated version. It's a letter from Mate Boban. If I could just focus your attention on the third and four paragraph, and I'll just read while you're looking at it. It says: "Still convinced that the principles of the negotiations under the patronage of the European Community are the only the possible way for the establishing of the government of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the war still can be stopped, it is necessary to apply at once some of the agreed principles of the future constitutional arrangements of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then Mr. Boban goes on to say: "Therefore, we suggest that instead of disintegrated and illegal authorities immediately a ministry council of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be mandated consisting of nine members, a party of the three people, as the European Community has proposed being the only authority of temporary governing Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, were you aware of this letter, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could just fast forward just for a little bit. We'll ahead of ourselves, in other words. At some other point there were some discussions while you were involved of having an interim or a temporary arrangement government where there would be nine, nine folks, three from each constituent peoples; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Vance-Owen Peace Plan, as we mentioned earlier, consisted of three main parts, and then after January 1993 the section for the interim government was incorporated into the plan. It's printed in the UN documents, and it was to be interim between the definitive acceptance of the Plan and the first elections of the new government. So that's why it was an interim government or sometimes called a provisional government. But, yes, there was -- there were provisions for an interim government under the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and you're correct, it envisaged a nine-member Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, there's been a lot of talk about Cutileiro, and we were able to dig up a letter to the editor in the Economist, and this is 1D 01315. And I thought I'd share this with you. This is a letter written by Mr. Cutileiro himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We don't have the exact date because of the way it's copied, but we'll -- we hope to get the original one for you, Your Honours, at some point, but if I could get the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're going to be moving rather quickly, sir, so we're going to need you on the double. Thank you. I think from the first couple of lines we could tell about what period of time this letter was written. It says: "Sir, in your article on Bosnia, November 25th, you say -- you say that in February 1992, before the war had started, Lord Carrington and I 'drafted a constitution that would have turned the country into a confederation of Swiss-style cantons. The Muslims refused to accept what they considered to be the disintegration of Bosnia.' Not quite. After several rounds of talks our 'principles for future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia and Herzegovina' were agreed by the three parties (Muslims, Serbs and Croats) in Sarajevo on March 18th as the basis for future negotiations. These continued, maps and all, until the summer when the Muslims reneged on the agreement. Had they not done so, the Bosnian question might have been settled earlier with less loss of (mainly Muslim) life and land. To be fair, Mr. Izetbegovic and his aides were encouraged to," looks like "scupper," "scupper that deal and to fight for unitary Bosnian state by well-meaning outsiders who thought they knew better." And it's signed Jose Cutileiro, Secretary-General, Western European Union, Brussels. Now, in looking at this letter to the editor, it would appear that he's correct as far as his interpretation of what the Cutileiro Plan envisaged, is he not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He doesn't say what they were. He just says the future constitutional arrangements were agreed. He does not say what those constitutional arrangements were. We looked at them yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he does say what it isn't, what the Cutileiro Plan is not. When he says not quite in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says not quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not quite. Okay. In any event, let's look at again the map, and what we've done last night in light of your testimony, we -- we thought we'd -- do you have it? You have it? We went out and we looked at -- we got the map and we have an overlay here of the Banovina of 1939 in light of the question that I posed to you, and you seemed to equivocate that, well, it did look like the Banovina and with this overlay it would appear, would it not, that the Cutileiro Plan does not look anything like the Banovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you yesterday, Mr. Karnavas, there was no definitive map. Therefore, the question really has no meaning, and I draw to your attention Ambassador Cutileiro's confirmation in the letter you just read where he talks of maps in the plural, because each side were giving maps and they were being developed, and they were of there were many maps as Ambassador Cutileiro said. There was no one map. So therefore, I can't answer a question that has no basis in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But as far as I understand, and it might be wrong and I'll being corrected if I am wrong, that the Croats did in fact sign this particular map, and as you indicated, you called them free-riders that willing to sign anything because they had nothing to lose, but as far as I understand they did in fact sign this map, and this map, along with the Cutileiro Plan, was presented prior to the referendum, was it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not sign this map with us. They signed the map of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. The map you're showing is what you call the Cutileiro Plan, March 1991. That was never at issue in Vance-Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not speaking about Vance-Owen. The reason I'm mentioning this, sir, is because you seem -- with all due respect, you characterise the Croats as these free-riders that were very similar to the Serbs with one an aim in mind, to ethnically cleanse the Muslims so they could carve out Bosnia so at some point they could have either an entity within the state or for that entity could be annexed to Croatia. That's your thesis. And what I'm suggesting here is, if we look at this proposed map and we put it over the Banovina, it don't like anything like the Banovina, and, two, if we look at it closely we even see that Mostar, that Mostar is not even given to the Croats at this particular time in this particular map. That's my thesis.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map has no standing, had no standing, never really existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless, it was the -- it was the Croats that did in fact sign Cutileiro. The Muslims did sign it but then reneged; correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not sign a map. They signed the constitutional principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Constitution principles.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we must keep that distinction, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant, but thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And may I recall as we read -- you read yesterday for us that the constitutional principles of the Cutileiro Plan called for three states within one state. It said that. Three -- three separate units based on the national principle, which meant ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute. That's your interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have -- that was the Croat interpretation of -- of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, and it surely would have been the Croat interpretation of -- of the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, now you seem to be speculating. As I recall yesterday, I asked you a question and you said to me, "that would be speculating." So we shouldn't go into that. So now you seem to be speculating as to what the Croats' intentions were. Here I've showed you a letter from Boban back in 1992 that he's saying, Let's get on with the Cutileiro. Let's go on with the European Community programme to avoid bloodshed, to avoid war. And this is -- it seems -- I don't see how you make that leap, but we'll go step-by-step. Now, speaking of borders, it wasn't that the Croats were the ones that were initiating the discussion on changing the borders. It seems to me if we look at David Owen's book, and just an excerpt of it, 1D 00894.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And my point here is, for Your Honours, is here the European interlocutors are also the ones talking about the borders not being sacrosanct, which begs the question: Who is initiating or who is raising this issue, is it Tudjman the historian turned president or is it the Europeans who are trying to find a pragmatic solution. If we look at this paragraph, chapter 2, if you look down to the first -- second paragraph it says: "The Netherlands have held the EC Presidency from the outbreak of the war," and then it goes on -- I don't want -- I'll skip to where it says: "The Dutch government had suggested to the other EC Member States that the option of agreed change to some of the internal borders between the Yugoslav republics might be explored." And then to save time, if you look to the next page, well, the very same page but it's -- it will be 33 on his book, to bullet point 4, it says: "The foregoing seems to point to the direction of a voluntary redrawing of internal borders as a possible solution." And we don't have time, but it would seem to me if we were to read the rest of the -- rest of the chapter, especially focusing on page number -- page 36 of this particular chapter, it would appear that the Europeans themselves, the negotiators, are talking about that perhaps the borders could be changed although it was recognised that that might be opening a Pandora's box and best to let it be as it is.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should clarify your comments, Counsel, by noting that the borders that were being discussed here were the republic borders, not borders within the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that. I understand that. But what I'm saying -- your thesis, sir, has been that Tudjman, who was the highest Croat controlling all of those Croats was intent on carving up Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would have been one of the republics. And what I'm pointing out to you, sir, is that the Europeans themselves had talked about perhaps we should tinker around with the borders within the republics. This is as Yugoslavia is breaking up.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said they were talking of tinkering with the borders within the republics. That is incorrect. They were talking about the borders between the republics, not within the republics, as you stated. That is simply not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understand the difference, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand the difference. At some point Croatia becomes an independent country, does it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It ceases to be a republic at that point, a republic within Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Bosnia and Herzegovina also becomes an independent country; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Declares itself to be independent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so -- now, prior to that there's a whole discussion going on about the break-up of Yugoslavia; right? Which is composed of - what is it? - five different republics?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it's within this context that the republican borders might be changed. I mean, it calls for a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion never advanced very far. Lord Owen was somebody who thought about it, but there were never ever even borders changes physically proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an idea, a loose idea that diplomats and negotiators think of as they think of all options when they look at a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's my whole --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in no case were they ever talking about redrawing of borders within any of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not saying within any of the republics. Sir, don't steer the conversation away. What I'm trying to suggest to the Trial Chamber here is that there seems to be from the Prosecution and from you a thesis that it was Tudjman that is -- can't wait along with Milosevic to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what I'm suggesting to you as -- as Yugoslavia is breaking up, some folks are thinking outside the box, and those folks happen to be the Europeans, you know. And this is 13 July 1991 now. And while you might say, well, this is just a bunch of discussions, that we were just thinking about it as we would normally do, what I'm trying to demonstrate to the Trial Chamber is, this is not something that Tudjman was initiating or even Milosevic but even the Europeans are thinking that perhaps one way to resolve the break-up of Yugoslavia is to see whether the republican borders can be changed, and it was decided that best to leave them as they are because that would open up a Pandora's box.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The European Community decided to retain the borders of the republics. They decided that early on, already in 1991, and they decided it on the basis of the Helsinki agreement of 1975, which called for the non-alteration, the non-alteration, of borders in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there were individuals who toyed with all kinds of ideas, but the idea of changing the borders never had any official standing at any time, as you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I have said. Okay. Very well. Let's move on. Now, yesterday we talked a little bit about the Muslim government even at that particular time, that is in 1992, was -- or the government in Bosnia-Herzegovina was being perceived as a Muslim-dominated government or a Muslim government, and I want to share with you 1D 00814. This is a speech by Lord Owen. It's -- it's dated 16 December 1992. 16 December, 1992. And if we look at the third paragraph from the top it says: "One of our concerns is that the -- is that the Bosnia and Herzegovina government is sadly increasingly becoming representative only of a Muslim population. We are travelling tomorrow to Zagreb to meet with President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic in an attempt to bring together the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats into a more representative Presidency. We will try, though we know it will be very difficult to persuade both sides to come to some measure of agreement on a provisional map for Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, did you share at that point in time, in history, that is 16 December 1992, Lord Owen's impression? After all he is giving a speech now and delivering it, concerning his observations. And this would be at the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. Did you share his impressions that the Bosnia-Herzegovina government was increasingly becoming representative only of the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I so stated that in my witness statement. May I call your attention very briefly to paragraph 11 where I say in the -- in my witness statement that the powers, as well as the activities of the government are severely limited. It was clear to the negotiators during the lengthy negotiations that President Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, and Akmadzic were representing the government officially while Izetbegovic and Silajdzic were mainly representing Bosnian Muslim interests, and Akmadzic was mainly representing Bosnian Croat interests. That is in my witness statement of March. You have that. So that's what I agree. And Lord Owen is correct, and my witness statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I appreciate the confirmation you provide by quoting Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Now, there were others also that thought that this was -- this government, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was for all intents and purposes representing only, if not exclusively, the Muslim agenda.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say not exclusively but mainly. Surely mainly the Muslim agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So during these negotiations when Izetbegovic would show up with Silajdzic, with Ganic and others, he -- he is more concerned about his agenda as the leader of the SDA and the leader of the Muslim people as opposed to the well-being of all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would you say that is correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you restate the question? I didn't hear it well. .

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When Mr. Izetbegovic is -- is attending these meetings and is negotiating, he is negotiating primarily, if not exclusively, for the Muslim interests and not for the well-being of every citizen living in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part of your statement is correct, but the second part is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was representing mainly the Muslim interests because, again, they were being attack. Sarajevo was being shelled. The Serbs had grabbed 70 per cent of the country. We must remember that, and I know you do, but this was wartime. But it's incorrect to say that he wasn't concerned about the well-being of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. There were some that were even questioning the legality of this -- of this government as being a government that represented, you know, the country itself. Would you -- would that be a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That people challenged the legality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Serbs did, and the Bosnian Croats did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you feel that this was the government for Bosnia and Herzegovina representing the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we were very well aware of all of the problems inside the Bosnian government, and we knew when to distinguish between nation-wide desiderata and Muslim, Croat, and Serb desiderata.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, normally I would go through your diary step-by-step but we don't have the time, so instead we will look at it some time later. We will focus on January and then we're going to move to April and I want to go through some -- some various documents, some you might have seen and some maybe you haven't, but we can move it -- move through them rather quickly. First, if we could look at 1158. This would be P, P I guess 01158. It's a Prosecutor document. If you could assist the Ambassador, please. 1158. This is the minutes from January 15, 1993. This is the presidential transcript. And if you could refresh my memory. Were you there at that particular meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was probably in Geneva chairing the conference, but you could consult my diary and that would be -- the answer there would be. They took Ahtisaari with them so I probably was chairing the conference in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly we're going to touch on a few things to highlight, and of course the Trial Chamber will have -- will be able to read this at its leisure. If we look at page 4. You have Dr. Franjo Tudjman saying: "I agree that Posavina is more important than this, but how can we achieve peace? That's the problem. So we must compromise when the warring sides are concerned. All of them must compromise if we want peace."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is on page 4, and it's the -- you'll see at the bottom of the page in the middle, they have numbers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to help you out here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We are not seeing it either on the page 4 of 1158.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there must be a technical problem or maybe there's a -- this is a Prosecution document. Is that right, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The document we have under that number are minutes from the talks between the president of the republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, et cetera, Cyrus Vance, Lord Owen, Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And on page 4, on the top we have Ahtisaari and he seems to be speaking on that page alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. There's page 2, page 3, page -- if you put it on the ELMO that might assist but there's a page in the middle of the page it says, Your Honour, Alija Izetbegovic, Franjo Tudjman, and then again Alija Izetbegovic. It's four pages into the text. Have you found it, Your Honour? Well, we have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it is page 11 on our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 11. It can't be. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It starts with, "Mr. Tudjman reported as saying, 'I agree that Posavina is more important than this.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Obviously my pages are wrong. I don't know what the problem is, and we may have some problems with this document. But, okay. But thank you for pointing that out, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, here we see that Mr. Tudjman is concerned about the warring sides and he's urging them to compromise; correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so -- and you think that he wasn't earnest when he was stating that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was always concerned about Croatian interests and Croat interests. That was no surprise. He would have wished, of course, to achieve his goals by peace. Everybody does. Every political leader wants to achieve his goals peacefully. There were many goals needless to say that President Tudjman didn't care about, you know, areas that were Serb or Serb-Muslim areas. For example, Sarajevo. You know, less than 10 per cent of the population of Sarajevo were Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So he just -- he didn't -- wasn't concerned. But naturally they're all going to say they want peace, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. So everybody is lying at this table.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, but if I get your impression, and I don't mean to be confrontational, but with all due respect, Mr. Ambassador, you are painting a picture that everyone, with the exclusion of maybe Alija Izetbegovic, and you and Vance and Owen, all of them are liars?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That none of them are there with goodwill. None of them are there trying to solve of problems.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They all had interests and they were trying to advance their interests. It is your statement that they were lying, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would peace be -- would -- well, you've indicated in your diary who's lying and who's not, at times, or at least who is being characterised as liar, but would you agree that at this point in time, in January, it was also in the interests of Croatia to -- to stop the war are in Bosnia because it was draining their resources as well. They were having to -- to house all these refugees. You had Croatians getting killed in -- in Bosnia. You had the international community screaming up and down. So wouldn't it be natural for him to want peace at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They, the Bosnian Croats, as we all know in this courtroom, had signed all the sections of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan on January 2. I've already stated that. And that, of course, was welcomed by us and the negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary for us to go any more into this January 15th since you weren't there, but you seem to indicate that perhaps Mr. Tudjman did not have good intentions. At least that's what I'm reading from your statement -- from your testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. That is your extrapolation, and it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for pointing that out. If we could look at 1D 01312. This is a Security Council report, and this is -- I'm going to go through -- go back in history and then go forward. This is 11 November 1992. I hope I get the page right this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you look at -- on the left-hand side of the page, upper part, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page you'll see "Diplomatic activities," paragraph 14. I hope I have it right this time.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here it says: "The co-chairmen have engaged in extensive diplomatic activities ..." And then I'm going to skip to the very last words of the paragraph on this page. It says going to the next page: "They have been in steady contact with the principal leaders in the former Yugoslavia as well as the leaders of the neighbouring countries. They have contacted governments in a position to assist the peace process and have been -- and have brought together at Geneva Presidents Cosic and Tudjman on one hand, and Presidents Cosic and Izetbegovic on the other. They have also sought to deal with the central relation ship between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in light of last year's bitter conflict between Croats and Serbs, whose aftermath is still felt. The co-chairmen have also given close attention to the potentially explosive situation in the Serbian province of Kosovo, and Macedonia." So the only point I wish to make here is that it would appear that the co-chairmen, at least if we are to believe them in this report to the Security Council are saying that they are contacting leaders of neighbouring countries for their assistance. They have contacted governments in a position to assist the peace process. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is so stated and it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the neighbouring countries in this conflict at the time would have been Croatia, would it not have been?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not have considered Croatia a neighbouring country because Croatia was part of ex-Yugoslavia. When they are talking about neighbouring countries here, and I made missions to the countries. I'm personally familiar with what they're talking about, they meant Italy, Vienna, Austria. Those were the neighbouring countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in constant contact, of course, with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to the next document, and this is P -- I guess it would be 00752, or 752. This is a Security Council Resolution 787, dated 16 November 1992. We'll go through it very quickly. 752, that is. That's the Exhibit number. On the very first page, in the middle, I'll just -- I'm just going to go through a couple of sections of this document. In the middle it says: "We are confirming it's firm support for the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia as the framework within the overall political settlement of the crisis in the former Yugoslavia may be achieved. And for work of the co-chairmen of the steering committee ..." then it goes on. We'll go on to the next page. Well, starting the bottom of the first page it says "noting," and then the very last sentence where it says bullet point number 4, "the establishment of a Mixed Military Working Group in the province of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the production of a draft outline constitution for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then if you go further down where it says: "Calls upon the parties in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to consider the draft outline constitution as a basis for negotiating a political settlement of the conflict in that country, and to continue negotiations for constitutional arrangements on the basis of the draft outline," and it goes -- and so on. Next page, bullet number 3: "Strongly reaffirms," and then it goes on, "to respect strictly the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then we skip number 4, we go to number 5. "Demands," sort of the last sentence. It talks about -- and this might be interesting here, including the last three lines I'm going to read, "including the requirement that all forces, in particular elements of the Croatian army be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or shall disbanded or disarmed." And then it goes on to talk about welcoming the report. At this point in time, sir, was the HVO one of the recognised armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Recognised army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was -- we knew of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's recognised in the sense of officially sanctioned, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was it ever sanctioned as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could -- excuse me. My I comment re: Something that you've drawn to the attention of the Court and I want the president and the Judges --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer back to paragraph 3 that you started reading but you didn't finish it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads in its entirety: "Strongly reaffirms its call on all parties and others concerned to respect strictly the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's where you ended so I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "And affirms that any entities unilaterally declared or arrangements imposed in contravention thereof will not be accepted," and that is a specific reference to Republika Srpska and to the community of Herceg-Bosna, because they were precisely the units that were declared. So here you have already in November, and I'm pleased that you draw this to our attention, that already at the highest international level in a Resolution of the Security Council the very existence of these self-declared entities, Herceg-Bosna, Bosnian Croats, Republika Srpska for the Serbs, was in contravention, was condemned, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as far as you're concerned it was an entity. It was an entity like Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It had the same attributes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had a president. It had officers. They issued statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware at all whether -- under the constitution, whether the municipalities could -- could join together to form and community, for instance, in -- in time of need? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware at all of the All People's Defence, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old people's?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All, A-l-l, All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The All People's Defence. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you aware? It calls for a yes or no, and if you are, tell us; if not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all kind of units sometimes 8 or 10 people in the town, Mr. Karnavas, so there were lots of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- so in other words you're not aware that built into the constitutional framework of the former Yugoslavia and then down to the republics there was a concept of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which also included the Territorial Defences?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were Territorial Defence units in the former Yugoslavia and All People's Defence surely referred to combatting a foreign invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're pretty safe in -- in coming to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, it would appear that from these resolutions they're asking the parties to cooperate; correct? And we're going to read some more, but it would appear that they're asking the parties to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if Croatia cooperates, it seems to me they're damned because they're free-riders. At least that's what you want us to conclude that no matter what the Croats do, if they're positive and they're being urged to cooperate, they're free-riders, but then if they had, if they did not cooperate, I'm sure you would be saying they were obstructing just as the Serbs were.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, my question is don't you find that rather cynical to say that they're free-riders when at the same time you're asking them to cooperate and they're cooperating?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't find it cynical in the least, because the fact is, Mr. Karnavas, that the document you've introduced here we're reading is November, already just a month earlier, three weeks, actually, towards the end of October, the Croats -- Bosnian Croat forces had carried out a very heavy ethnic cleansing operation around Prozor. So I'm just describing the -- their actions, which were not in conformity with their words. Sometimes there were. Very often there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go on to 932, document P 00932. And this is a document of the general -- from the General Assembly. It's dated 17 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, what is the number? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 932. 932. This would be a Prosecution document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm just going to -- if we just look at the bottom of the page it says, "taking note," and I'm going to skip and go into the next page to the one, two, three, the fourth paragraph: "Recalling that the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has accepted the constitutional principles proposed by the co-chairmen of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia." Okay? Was that correct, that the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had -- had accepted the constitutional principles proposed by the co-chairmen? This is now 18 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And then if we go further down in the page we'll see a number 1: "Reaffirms its support for the government and people of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then number 4 it says: "Demands --" we can step -- next page I'm sorry go to the next page to number 5: "Demands also that in accordance with the Security Council Resolution 752 all elements of the Croatian army that may be in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that are already not operating in accords with the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina must be withdrawn immediately or be subject to the authority of the government or be disbanded." Again, we -- I asked you earlier whether the HVO was ever recognised as legitimate armed force within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe you said that you were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't. They're talking about the army of the republic of the Croatia. They're not talking about the HVO here. This is clearly a reference to the army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, if the HVO, as far as you understand, the HVO was never part -- was never recognised as a legitimate force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as you know, being a negotiator at that period of time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we dealt with it. We knew the people who were in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That wasn't my question sir.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, that isn't the answer to my question, and you know very well. I'm asking: Was it ever recognised as a legitimate force? It calls for a yes or a no. You could have been negotiating with an illegitimate force because those were the only people that you could negotiate with. But I'm asking you: Were you aware yes, or no, whether the HVO was ever recognised as a legitimate force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that would have been recognised by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have been at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry, the answer is: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is the answer I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The answer is, "it might have been." "It might have been" means to me that I'm taking a wild guess.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't take wild guesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I think we can skip the rest in that document, save some time. We can go on to the next document and this would be 1D 01313, 1313. That's 1D 01313 this is to the Security Council. Now we're up to December 24, 1992, and if I could focus everyone's attention it would be on page 8, that is the page 8 as is designated so on the upper left-hand side of the page. And I'll be referring to primarily paragraph 29. This section deals with maps and I just wanted to draw to everyone's attention paragraph 29 it says: "The Bosnian Croat delegation submitted a map merely indicating those territories, consisting of one large, one medium-sized and four small ones, within the Croat allegedly constituted a majority of 60 per cent or more. No indication was given as to how provincial boundaries might be drawn in that light, although in accompanying oral explanations it was stated that the Croats would expect to end up with two provinces and that other concentrations of Croat populations would necessarily be assigned to provinces with other majorities." Was that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wrote it I myself contributed to the drafting of this document, and I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words what the Croats were proposing was that some portion of its population within Bosnia-Herzegovina would be residing in provinces that were controlled by or governed by either the Muslims or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not quite right. They were not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not proposing. We were proposing and they were acceding, as it states. You see, it says as it was stated that the Croats would expect to end up. Indeed, they were very, very decently treated by the Vance-Owen map. So as we all know, they signed it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But -- did you what I --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as I have pointed out to you yesterday, that as a result of the multi-ethnicity aspect of the Vance-Owen map, 36 per cent of the Bosnian Serb population resided in non-Bosnian Serb majority provinces, 30 per cent of the Bosnian Muslims resided in non-Bosnian Muslim populous, and 29 per cent of the Serbs. So that all of the parties had to accept, not just the Bosnian Croats as an act of goodwill. All of the parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had to accept --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understood that yesterday and I understand it today, and if you look at paragraphs 27 and 28, we're talking about the various delegations submitting maps.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not talking about the Vance-Owen map that you were proposing. And what I'm suggesting here, what I hope the Trial Chamber will understand, is that here are the Croats making their proposal, and in their proposal it is understood by them that, you know, a certain amount of Croats within Bosnia and Herzegovina will be residing in provinces that are controlled or governed by the Serbs -- the Serbs or the Muslims based on what we read on paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- you said not controlled and then you corrected yourself to say governed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also incorrect, because all of the -- all of the 10 provinces in the Vance-Owen Plan and they knew this at the time because we were discussing it with them were to be democratically organised. So one really can't speak and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the Muslims talked that way also and, of course, the Serbs did. So it wasn't just the Bosnian Croats. There was a tendency to say, This is our province.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, but -- and that's -- thank you for correcting me, and I --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't mean to correct you because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's -- it's very easily -- one can very easily slip into that kind of locution, but if we're talking about the plan, then we have to recognise that the plan envisaged a thoroughly democratic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But some provinces would be allocated to the Serbs. Some provinces would be allocated to the Croats or would be designated as Croat-dominated. However you wish to point it out.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would have a majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were ten provinces. Four had no majority whatsoever. Six had a majority of one of the three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're correct when you say they would have a majority, but it's just unfair to the plan to talk of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- and I --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know you don't mean it, so I'm just trying to correct it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the -- so that we all -- the Court and all of us have a correct understanding of the plan. I don't mean to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- contentious at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're not. Trust me. 1D 01314. That's our next document. 1D 01314. This is dated 6 January 1993. And again I just want to point a couple of things out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm doing this for the Trial Chamber's benefit because we don't have a whole lot of time to go -- to have these lengthy discussions but merely to show that there is some continuity in what is happening on the ground. Now, if we could focus on page number 2, Your Honours. That would be paragraph 10. Just -- I'm going to read just a portion that is relevant, I think. In their opening address to the talks on 2 January, the co-chairmen, Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen, appealed to the participants that "This is an historic meeting. It is our best chance for peace and we must ensure that it succeeds." I think that's a -- everybody wanted that and that's a pretty accurate statement. Then if we go on to page 4, paragraph 18, this is about the Plenary Session at 4 January, 1993. At a Plenary Session of the talks on 4 January, the co-chairmen reminded the participants that the success or failure of the talks depend primarily on them. The ultimate choice was theirs, peace or war." And it goes on. Again I think that's more or less an accurate statement. Basically it's up to them. And then if we go on to paragraph 22, which would be on page 5, it says: "All the delegations participating in the talks pledged their cooperation with the co-chairmen and search for peaceful solutions. The peace process has thus taken -- taken on a qualitatively new dimension. Henceforth it should be easier to establish clearly who is cooperating and who is not. I believe that the Security Council should let it be known clearly to all sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina that it is their duty to cooperate with the co-chairmen in bringing the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina to it and end swiftly and that there would be penalties for obstruction." Now, I raise this because, again, at least based on Mate Boban's attitude, it would appear -- and we'll go through your diary at some point, but it would appear that he's the one that's always at the meetings, ready, willing, and indeed able to sign the peace proposals.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've discussed this extensively yesterday so I can summarise it very briefly. In January, I helped draft this statement. I'm very familiar with it. I was there, and I can -- I know what was in Mr. Vance's mind, but I know better still the facts on the grounds. In January, yes, the Bosnian Croats had signed the agreement and, yes, they were conducting ethnic cleansing operations in Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. They were doing both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever visit Bosnia and Herzegovina during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you go to Mostar, for instance? Go to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I was in Mostar and rarely -- rarely in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. One second here. Do you know by chance how many Muslim refugees there were in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In January, yeah.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Herzegovina alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly; no, I don't know. I could make a guess but it would only be a questions, and I would not wish to have you remonstrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you. All right. If we can go on - I'm moving rather quickly - to the transcript of January 20, 1993. This is 1D 01311. I believe it's an entire transcript, and I don't recall, but I'm sure you'll remind us, whether you were there at the time. This would be January 20, 1993. Do you recall whether you were there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, I believe. It's in -- we can check my diary, but I'm pretty sure I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the day, incidentally, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- began in Zagreb and ended in Sarajevo, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And that was the day that Clinton was sworn in?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was being sworn in, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And you were warning him to be careful because it would appear that based on the presidential elections they seemed to be at least their campaigning going on that they had some ideas as to how they might be able to deal with the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. During the campaign, the Clinton campaign took a very -- took a much more aggressive position on the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and accused the outgoing republican administration of negligence, cowardice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sort of thing. They said they would be much more ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Robust?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Robust in their policy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I wrote, "Clinton, be careful." And I think you would even agree with that actually but I'm not asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could -- if we look at page 2. It's number 2, page number 2 at the top -- at the top page, Your Honours, and I'm going to go through it very quickly. Here there seems -- from the previous page we know that it's -- that it's -- President Tudjman is speaking, and he's -- and he's bringing up an issue which is an accusation that is being lodged against Croatia by Izetbegovic. I just want to point this out because it appears that later on if we go into page 8, he is asking -- he's asking the -- I believe Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, he's asking them how he should respond, and that's on the -- on page 8 where it says: "If I may, I would suggest we hear your opinion from BiH. What do you think how should Croatia react to these accusations? And I would especially request the opinion of the gentlemen, co-chairmen, because this is tied to a general consideration on the crisis of Bosnia-Herzegovina," and he goes on. In essence he's asking them, how -- how should he as president of the Republic of Croatia respond to these public accusations by -- by Alija Izetbegovic. And this concerns Alija Izetbegovic's accusations that the HV, that is the Croatian army, was involved or responsible for Gornji Vakuf. And if we go to page 9, I just want to draw this out to the Trial Chamber's attention, Lord Owen says in response: "Mr. President -- Mr. President, you asked me how the Croatian government should react. I think that your response should be guided by the principle you yourself have formulated and expressed more than once and that is that peace is of the highest interest to the -- to the Republic of Croatia and therefore I think that regardless of today's or rather the latest news the tensions and the heat created in the public should be reduced. I of course have no desire to tell you, "and then it goes on and on and on. And I -- so it appears that Lord Owen is counselling the president to react the way he has in the past. Now, was Lord Owen being cynical at this point or was he being earnest?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was being a -- first if I may say this: I misspoke when I said we were in Zagreb first on the 20th and then Sarajevo. It was the reverse. It was the meeting in Sarajevo and then on to Zagreb to see President Tudjman to give him a precise of the meeting. You will recall very briefly from yesterday's discussion that this was the meeting where there was a heated discussion between Izetbegovic, really an argument, almost a shouting match, although he did not shout, but pretty close, between Izetbegovic and Mile Akmadzic, and it's the meeting at which he started by reading from prepared notes. He had a prepared statement and the argument was basically about Gornji Vakuf. That's correct. And Lord Owen here is appealing to the senior Croatian authority, we've already discussed whether President Tudjman was the senior authority in -- for the Bosnian Croats, and he was, and I've elucidated on that and explained it to you, and here Lord Owen, of course, confirms it, and basically he's saying please, you know, issue another statement, and we will try and bring you together with Izetbegovic and see if we can't work this out, and we did. That's -- if you consult my diary, you'll see that a few days later we had Izetbegovic and President Tudjman together, and of course we also brought in, when it was necessary, Slobodan Milosevic, because he was the boss of Radovan Karadzic. But I should say that the -- and this is an important point, so please allow me just half a minute. On the question of command and control, we went into this quite a bit over the last few days, there's no doubt that Milosevic was in charge of the Bosnian Croat [sic] operation, but he was not in complete charge. Even those who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, you do not want to say that Milosevic was in charge of the Croat operations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Yes, Judge, I meant Bosnian Serb. Thank you very much. Oh, dear. He wasn't in complete charge even though Serbia armed the Bosnian Serb army, paid them, sent them their gasoline and supplies. They were -- they had individual responsibilities and they were on the ground, so they had a measure of freedom of movement. So, too, President Tudjman was the boss, but that did not mean that he wrote every detail of Mate Boban's operation, and so Mate did have a freedom of movement on -- you know, on many points. They knew each other. They trusted each other. Gojko Susak and Mate were both from -- knew each other from Grude, and so it's important to understand that when we talk about President Tudjman being the very important person that he was, that he still wasn't responsible for everything. Excuse me. Thank you for allowing me to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm pressed for time but again as I pointed out yesterday I don't see anything in your notes, your 2.000-page diary anything of that nature but --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary is full of it. There I must -- I must be categorical and I have to disagree with you, counsel. I'm very sorry. The diary indicates that clearly. I know what's in my diary. I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During the break I urge you to go through your diary and point out concretely where you say that Tudjman is controlling Boban, where Tudjman is in charge of the HVO. Try to find something, because as I said, in your previous three testimonies you've never raised that, and I dare say it appears that you've come here with a brief, a brief to sort of carry, and that's -- and that's why it appears that you're volunteering all this information that's nowhere anywhere in your notes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all over my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Excuse me. I have been quiet today, but I'm going to have to object to that last comment. That goes way too far. He's just very explicitly accused the witness of having been scripted and coming here, without a basis, to give the answers that he's given. Secondly, I think -- I submit that the Ambassador yesterday very thoroughly and very clearly answered the question that is -- when he testified in other cases, and I think that -- I think it can resonate with the Chamber, when he testified in other cases, in the Milosevic case, there was no point for him to come in here and start talking about his dealings and his views about Tudjman. It was irrelevant in those case, as if I had gone into one of those other cases - if I had gone into one of those other cases -- if I'd gone into the Milosevic case and started talking about Dario Kordic. It made no difference. So this is a completely -- number one, it's a false issue, and, number two, and more importantly, I object to attacking this man for having come here and giving supposedly scripted evidence. That's beyond the pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody said he was giving scripted evidence, but it's obvious, it's obvious from his testimony that it's not included in the notes or his prior testimony that for the first time we hear various new things. That's all I'm saying. So.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to tell you again it's in my notes. May I cite examples? I don't want to take your time but I can give examples right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay you don't want to hear it. I accept the fact that you do not want to hear what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during the break if you can find concretely in your notebook where you say that Boban is being instructed by -- by Tudjman or where Tudjman is controlling the HVO in the manner in which you state over here today, I would like to see that. Also, I would like to see where -- where there are reports, where you're concrete -- you, yourself are concretely making those allegations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not allegations. They are facts. May I just point out, why do you think Lord Owen, Secretary Vance, and I were in President Tudjman's office that evening of January 20th after Akmadzic and Izetbegovic had exchanged those vehement words? It was precisely because he was the boss and he -- we felt, even though it was pretty close to midnight, it was the end of a very long day, that it was important to inform him of what happened. Nothing could be clearer. What were we doing in President Tudjman's office? We didn't go there for any other reason except to assure him of what had happened, of our interpretation of that shouting match, I said, of the behaviour of Akmadzic, behaviour of Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I heard that, sir. We heard that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you hear it, but then you don't draw the conclusions, Mr. Karnavas. You keep saying, I've read your thousands of pages and it doesn't have a sentence that says Tudjman is the boss, but reality is reality, Mr. Karnavas. We were in his office on the night of January 20th because he was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again, as I say, where in your diary do you say that you and Vance and Owen went to visit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think -- I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have invited the witness to look it up during the break. I think it's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And we're losing your time when you nevertheless go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the last thing that I wanted to point out on January 20th is on page 20th -- on page 20 it's David Lord Owen is suggesting that it's time to think about or to talk about the transitional government or temporary government. Do you recall that part of the discussion?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this was the principle of 3, 3, 3; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we did indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Create as I've discussed earlier, we did set up a transitional -- an interim government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And this is the 3, 3 principle basically or this concept as we indicated was mentioned much earlier by Mate Boban -- Mate Boban when he was asking Cutileiro to come up with a solution. And this was back in, I believe, it was 19 --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the same. It was not Mate's concept because what you question implies -- I don't mean you're saying it in bad faith at all, but what it replies is that the interim government would replace the current Bosnian government headed by Alija Izetbegovic during the interim period, and that's not correct. The -- the government was to retain overall control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, we'll get to it later on, but -- but this interim government, one -- one of the sticking points was that Alija was insisting on being -- again, retaining that position; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He didn't want to give up.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he felt that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The answer is, no, he didn't want to give up?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He wanted -- he wanted to stay in power throughout this entire time when, in fact, months -- months leading up to this point everybody recognised that this government was not representative of all of the people but it was representative only of one constituent person -- peoples.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. During -- because of the war. But if the Vance-Owen Peace Plan had been accepted by the Serbs, if it had come into effect, then even with the -- President Izetbegovic remaining in power, of course the government would have been more representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, wartime does make a difference. So I've just tried to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. Now, if I could -- and I have to apologise here if we could go back to January 15, 1993, the presidential transcript, because there is an interesting exchange there with Gojko Susak. And this is -- I'm sorry, the ERN number is -- I guess it would be P 01158. P 01158, and in my pages, Your Honour, at the bottom it says 19. It's at the -- it's towards the end of -- it's three pages from -- from the last page. I apologise for having skipped over this point, but we might -- we might be able to cover it very quickly here before the break. In this exchange, while you're looking for it --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what page is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is on page 19. It's -- I don't know if the pages are correct, but --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But here, I -- we'll find it right here --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- copy.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the page. You'll see Gojko Susak is speaking, and he says, "I would just once again ask a purely practical question, and I thought we understood a long time ago. I spoke with you, President Izetbegovic here in Zagreb, and we spoke into front of the co-chairmen in Geneva too, and for the sake of efficiency in war, and we are in an unfavourable position anyway in an area with predominantly Muslim troops, and it has now been divided in provinces 2, the command over the army should be by BH and in areas with predominantly HVO forces the command should be by the HVO. "I cannot understand what's now contentious in this, to have a common interest to defend ourselves against our common enemy. Isn't that the part we have achieved? I sat with you in the room, in the hotel here at the Esplanade, when we made a gentlemen's agreement that you would work on this. I don't see what's contentious if in Gornji Vakuf, no matter if there are more Muslims or fewer Croats there, but it is in the territory controlled by the HVO, if orders now coming from Sarajevo are contradictory to orders from Mostar. Well, you're killing yourselves. Then the Serbs do not need to fight you any longer." Now, based on this passage, sir, it would appear at least that there seems to be some sort of gentlemen's agreement where Izetbegovic has agreed or it has been talked about for -- at least at the operational level, for one army to be subordinate to the others depending on who is in control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Susak says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what Susak says?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's dead. Izetbegovic is dead. You weren't there. I wasn't there, so all we have is Gojko Susak's words on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But at this meeting on the 20th -- on the 15th, we have -- Mr. Cyrus Vance is there, at least it says -- I don't know if Mr. Owen was there. Mr. Owen was there as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you'll notice counsel that Gojko talks about this fighting in Gornji Vakuf this is what this argument was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, work with me. Work with me, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know you want to go to Gornji Vakuf. We've heard a lost evidence about that so you're not here to inform us or elucidate on that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the statement of Gojko Susak says, I don't see what is contentious if in Gornji Vakuf no matter if there are more Muslims or fewer Croats. So that's exactly what the discussion was about. That's what Susak's talking about, that in a non-Croat majority area, that the Croats were cleaning out the and ethnically cleansing the Bosnian Muslims. That's what the argument was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, sir, I don't mean to be rude?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Be rude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if you read it, if you read it carefully it looks like there is an agreement. There's an agreement that in certain areas the HVO, the HVO would subordinate -- would subordinate itself to the ABiH and, in fact -- let me finish. And, in fact, yesterday I noticed when the Prosecution showed you this -- this document dated January 15th, what was not mentioned, what was not drawn tower attention and what you failed to volunteer was the fact that in that very same document HVO forces were being asked to subordinate themselves severs in ABiH in certain areas. Did you happen to notice that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it but I'm sure if you say it, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's -- the document was P 01155. We can bring it up real quickly. But in essence that document not only asked for the ABiH to subordinate itself to the HVO in certain areas, but also vice versa, that the -- that the -- the HVO would subordinate itself to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear at least that this sort of validates what the discussion is, that there is -- there seems to be some sort of a gentlemen's agreement but Izetbegovic seems to be reneging on this agreement, this gentlemen's agreement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, just one last document and then we're going to have to have the break, but just very quickly sticking with this point, and again P -- the one document that was brought to your attention now, which is P 01155, we've seen many, many times so I don't think there is a dispute. And I can be corrected by my colleague here if I misstated that in certain provinces the HVO was to subordinate itself to the ABiH. But let's look at a document 1D 00820. 1D 00820. And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour while that's being done I would like to correct the transcript to be pointed out and for it to be properly stated at one point in reference back -- it's left the main screen now but on page -- excuse me, Your Honour, one moment. On page 41, that was earlier on line 5, the language that Mr. Karnavas keeps referring to about a gentlemen's agreement, the exact language is, "a gentlemen agreement that you would work on this." It doesn't say anything about what the agreement was or whether there was such an agree -- something -- a gentlemen agreement to work on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, he could do this on redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, this the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you would kindly avoid overlapping, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can do this on redirect and he knows the rules. He knows the rules and he doesn't have to eat up my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is exactly the same kind of interruptions I get on direct, and when it's coming from the Defence, apparently it's okay. But when I do it on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honours, you have the documents. You have the documents. We're not in front of a jury. Nobody's trying to misrepresent anything. The gentleman was shown the document. There's no need to grandstand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at this, 1D 00820. This is dated 20 January 193 We've received this. What we've -- we've seen this once before.
