Were you aware of this at all this document that comes from Mate Boban and it seems to be faxed. There's -- we have the original. It's handwritten from the Intercontinental Zagreb. I assume that you've stayed there or are familiar with that particular hotel in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I normally stayed at the Esplanade but I'm -- you asked me the question. But I also stayed in the Intercontinental.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, here it appears that Mr. Boban is instructing the Croatian Defence Council that in reference to a decision 01132/93, and after the discussion with the co-chairmen of the Geneva conference of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Vance and Lord Owen, "I am ordering you to convene a special meeting of the HVO HZ HB during the day and change item 5 in a way to set up a deadline for the implementation of the decision." And then so --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what that could possibly be referring to since we have gone extensively over, and I certainly won't review it, the events of January 20th, Clinton's inauguration, the shouting match, the arguments back and forth. You have it in great detail in my diary, the January 20. I just can't tell you -- I cannot help you out on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps in honesty, I just have to say that to me it is not clear what item 5 mentioned here refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's why I was -- thank you. I thought -- I guess -- I'm assuming that everybody sort of knows where I'm going at but that's the wrong assumption on my part. I apologise. If we look at P 0115 -- 58, in the e-court. I'm sorry the document we need to be looking at is 1155. 1155. That was the decision of January 15th, 1993, and item 5, I believe, is where it talks about the various units subordinating in the various regions, and that's what it's referring to, Your Honour. And I believe we did discuss this on one previous occasion with the previous witness. I can't remember exactly off the top of my head with whom, but -- so when we look at 1155, I also think that at least down the road we should keep in mind 1D 00820. That's all I wanted to draw to the gentleman's attention. I note the time, Your Honour. Perhaps now would be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation into French to be over. It has been taking quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the two of you are speaking very fast, the interpreters are finding it very hard to follow, and that was the reason for the delay. We are going to take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to fast forward now, if I can, to -- to April, April 1993, and the first document we're going to look at, this covers, I believe, January, February, and March 1993. It's document P 1398, 1398. This is the Security Council official records, 48th year, supplement for January, February, and March. I know we touched on this a little bit but I'm focusing your attention again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On page 242, Your Honours. That would be -- looking at particularly paragraph 29, which is on page 242 of this particular document. The numbers are at the bottom. And here it's talking about the interim government that we previously touched upon earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In light of the ideas of intergovernmental arrangements put to the three sides by the co-chairmen, "President Izetbegovic, Minister for Foreign Affairs Silajdzic, Mr. Boban, and Prime Minister Akmadzic signed an agreement on 3 March 1993 which contained the following relevant provisions," and then it lists them. Is that correct? Was an agreement signed on March 3, 1993, for an interim government?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I also here that it only has the Croats and the Muslims signing, but the Serbs did not sign; correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The Serbs never signed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it envisaged that irrespective of what the Serbs were going to do or not do that the -- the Croats and the Muslims would go ahead and form an interim government?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole premise was -- of the peace plan was agreement by the three parties, the Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So basically Alija Izetbegovic didn't have to worry about moving along on the peace process, because I think it would be safe to say that everybody knew that the Serbs weren't going to agree to this interim government.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the degree that Izetbegovic knew and Boban knew and Tudjman knew and Vance knew and, you know, it was common knowledge that the Bosnian Serbs were recalcitrant and were not willing to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we all knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could go to document D -- P, I'm sorry, P 1924. This is a Security Council Resolution, 820, dated 17 April 1993. And I'll start with page 2. Under 1 it says it commends the peace plan. Number 2, welcomes the fact that the plan has now been accepted in full by two of the Bosnian parties. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll wait. I apologise for the pace, but it's just -- I don't want to go into one of my lectures about the lack of time, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think we do not have it. But I suggest that you go along so we do not disrupt your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for that, but maybe on the e-court they could locate it. It would be D -- P, P, P as in Paul, P as in Prosecutor. 1924.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's already on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1 it commends the peace plan 2 welcomes the fact that the peace plan has been accepted in full by two of the Bosnian parties. I'm going to skip down to number 7. "Reaffirms its endorsement of the principles that all statements or commitments made under duress, particularly those relating to land and property, are wholly null and void and that all displaced persons have the right to return in peace to their former homes and should be assisted to do so." Then we go to 8: "Declares its readiness to take all the necessary measures to assist the parties in the effective implementation of the peace plan once it has been agreed in full by the parties and requests the Security Council to submit to the council," going into the next page, "at the earliest possible date, and if possible not later than nine days after the adoption of the present resolution, a report containing an account of the preparatory work for the implementation of the proposal referred to in paragraph 28 of the Secretary-General's report 26 March 1993 (S/25479) and detail proposals for the implementation of the peace plan, including arrangements for the effective international control of the heavy weapons, based inter alia on consultations with Member States acting nationally or through regional organisations or arrangements." So here in this Resolution it is encouraging the implementation process once all parties have signed. Is that -- is that our understanding?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again the Croats have already signed, as have the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, again I want to go back. The fact that they have signed onto this Vance-Owen Peace Plan, might -- might an alternative plausible explanation to the ones that you have given us be that they -- that they have signed in earnest and in good faith?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that was belied by what was happening on the ground. In fact, mid-April was the period of perhaps the heaviest ethnic cleansing by the Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia. It even reached television. Pictures of activities, British troops, and UNPROFOR reported on it privately and publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So all one can say here, Mr. Karnavas, is that actions speak louder than words. We have that proverb in English. Actions speak louder than words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What were -- were the Muslims fighting at all?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were defending themselves, an and in certain -- in certain areas they were taking -- yes, they even took aggressive action. Those areas were mostly along the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Might -- might some of that action be against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely. It was mostly against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know where it might have been against the Croats and at what period? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were there any Croat refugees as a result of Muslim fighting?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm -- quite certainly there must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, but you don't know. I mean, must have been, and, of course, there was a war going on, but you seem to be telling us that you know of all the things that the Croats were doing and I'm asking you very simple: Do you know what the Muslims were during in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reason, Mr. Karnavas, that we know is we saw it on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see, okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the HVO it was shown widely, internationally, the events in Ahmici. I don't know if that's come up in this court but that's one town I remember seeing on the television. There was a town called Stupni Do where we -- with the television we saw it. So, yes, we know. Unless you're accusing the television networks of staging these events. You know, I wasn't -- I mean, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Nobody's being that cynical. All I'm asking you, sir, because you're the ambassador at the time, you're going around, I'm asking you concretely: Can you tell us, do you know whether any Muslim forces were attacking Croats and whether there were any Croat refugees as a result of actions taken by the ABiH against the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suggest you consult the reports that you have here of the European Community Monitoring Mission and UNPROFOR. My job was to negotiate, and I think you can understand I spent most of my time with the parties at the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a military observer. That was not my function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We receive the reports from the European Community Monitoring Mission, and that's UNPROFOR, but I don't think there's any surprise in what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go on to the next document, and that's another presidential transcript. It's a P 2059. This is dated 24 April 1993. It seems that we have president -- President Tudjman, Lord Owen. There's Izetbegovic. There's Boban. And very -- were you there by any chance? You don't have it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And I'm going to be directing everybody's attention to page 30. You will find the pages, they are on the right-hand bottom of the page. There are lots of things to cite in this document, but we don't have time, and -- but I just want to mention one point. Page 30, David -- Lord David Owen, it says here, he is speaking: "Rarely in my life have I hesitated more to say something than I do now. I've asked to mediate in this tragic episode but nobody obviously listens to my advice." And then it goes on. Again, for the sake of time, I don't want to waste it. Now, it goes on towards the bottom of the page, it says: "But -- but you can show that you want to plan and you can, if you want, to take the opportunity to change some of its parts before it is sign. This would be my best piece of advice." And then it goes on last paragraph: "As for a Joint Command, I think that more political common sense is needed here. It seems to me that there has been more constructiveness and a better tone at the military level than at the political one. This is an objective fact. I think that the problem lies with the Presidency and the structure of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these problems are extended further down. "If you don't solve it, you'll continue to have difficulties. If you don't address the problem seriously, it can cause great damage." And I think we can leave it at that. I don't want to go any further, take up more time, but it seems that at least Lord Owen is saying that the problem lies with the Presidency and the structure of the government. That's his interpretation. Do you share that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we've discussed this, that the government, that Izetbegovic and Silajdzic, as I stated in my witness statement, acted on behalf of the Muslims, and Akmadzic on the Croats, the government, and I think you cited it yesterday, I believe, or maybe the Prosecutor did, but there was a comment of mine, my own comment in one of my official diaries that the government was fictional. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fig leaf, yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, yes, I agree with it. And, you know, there were no angels in this process. Nobody has ever maintained that they were -- that the Muslim government or the Muslims were angels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at -- if you also look at some of your notes, it appears that Silajdzic at times was playing games. And I'm being kind of kind to the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was just trying to flesh out your comment. I don't know that I call it playing games. He was highly emotional, highly intelligent, certainly knew where he was going. So there were times when he dissembled for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there were times when -- excuse me. I apologise for that. Well, there were times also where Izetbegovic was vacillating back and forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He would agree to something and then later on disagree?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we've already seen his reneging on the Cutileiro Plan in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But -- and there was sort of exasperating at times was it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire process was exasperating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it would appear, at least to the other sides, that they were not acting in good faith. That's one plausible conclusion that one could reach.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And incidentally, I just want to go back to this document of April 24, 1993. I want to thank my colleague for pointing this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to page 3, Your Honours, and going on to page 4, again it's Lord Owen, he has started speaking on page 2, but if we go to page 3 he -- I'll just read it very quickly. "I don't think that it would be wrong to say that I have the best access to objective information in view of what was behind this episode and all those present in the room." These are the events dealing in Central Bosnia in April. He goes on to say - this is page 4, Your Honours - I'll skip the first paragraph: "If I thought that only one side was guilty, I would say so without hesitation. However, I'd like to say that in my opinion everybody has contributed to what has happened." So it would appear, would it not, that at least Lord Owen is saying based on objective information that he has access to, that the events in Central Bosnia in April can be attributed to both sides and not one. At least that's what he's saying. You don't have to agree or disagree, but ...

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me actually whether he's talking about the physical events or the -- in Central Bosnia here, or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay but let's go --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or the disagreement on command and control structure that we've discussed. I was at this meeting. I made extensive notes in my diaries. I would -- I would consult my diaries if I were you to find out the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We may -- we may get to that, pending time. But if we go on to the next paragraph he says: "However, I'd like to propose that we ensure that the meeting does not come down to pointing fingers at one another but, rather, in the first place that we look at each other and deal with the future." And then he goes on to say: "Generals Petkovic and Halilovic have spent several hours together this evening along with three objective, impartial advisors, more precisely two UNPROFOR generals and my personal military advisor, and as far as I know they have honestly and really conscientiously discussed this -- the issue." But needless to say, at least whatever it is that they're discussing, Lord Owen is blaming both sides.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll leave it at that. And it was it, I believe during this period, this particular event, where there was a break and the parties ended up drafting a -- a joint statement that we saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was a very long meeting.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all long meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can imagine. Okay. I'm going to switch to another topic, and we're going -- I'm going to go to a set of documents that are in Lord Owen's book Balkan Odyssey. These books are accompanying -- there was a CD apparently with one of the books when the book was originally published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm referring to a packet of documents Your Honours. It's 1D 01318. 1318. There are several documents. We don't have time to go through all of them. We'll go through some of them. Perhaps you might give us your impressions. If we look at page 264, which is page 2, actually, in the bundle that you have. We'll wait for Judge Trechsel. I believe he's searching to locate this. Do you have them, Your Honour? They would have been provided to you today. Yesterday, sorry. Yesterday. Do you have the documents, Your Honours? It's 1318. 1D 01318.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have it? I have an extra copy just in case. You have it. Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we turn the first page you'll see the next page is 264, and we look at the top. It's from Lord Owen's party, a private secretary to UK EC Presidency, 9 November 1992. And if we just look at the -- it's at the top of the page of the I just want to look at a couple of things. It says: "Bosnian Foreign Minister Silajdzic called Vance on 18 November to say Izetbegovic and the Bosnian government were outrage at the French proposal. They would certainly have expected to be consulted on an idea such as this. The French were in league with the Serbs who since they did not like the constitutional proposals now wanted to topple the Geneva conference. Suggestion was an attempt to do just that and represented a threat to the authority of the co-chairmen." Question: Were you aware of this communication?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever saw the communication. I was aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That led to this communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what was the French proposal that so irritated Mr. Silajdzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'll recall that on the 27th of October, 1992, just 10 days before this cable was drafted, that on 27 October 1992 the co-chairmen presented the constitutional principles for the first time to the three parties, and the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims agreed and the Serb did not, and this was the first, if we might say, dramatic, visible sign of Serb non-cooperation with the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. And a few days later, the French, in what may or may not have been a good faith proposal suggested things to the effect, "Well, since you can't get agreement, you know, let's have another ministerial conference." In other words, kick the problem upstairs to the level of the foreign ministers and we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the -- Silajdzic, the Bosnian Muslim and Foreign Minister of the government, reacted very negatively to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was this -- if you recall in history, because I recall reading about -- I might even remember actually seeing it at some point in time President Mitterrand had gone to Sarajevo, had he not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and Mrs. Mitterrand was with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was -- and he got as far as, I believe, the airport and then there was -- but in any event, was this before or after?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was well after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well after that. And could we not say that the fact that you have the president of France coming over there at that period of time was an act of good while of the French trying, you know, to assist the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was President Mitterrand. I assume he wanted to see for himself the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs were shelling Sarajevo, so the presence of senior western people, Mr. Vance, Lord Owen, Mitterrand, Mrs. Ogata of the UNHCR, that was a sign of solidarity with the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And I guess the reason I mention it is now we have Silajdzic not too long later accusing the French of being in the pockets of the -- of the Serbs or the Serbs being in the pockets of the French, whichever way you want to put it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's generally true. The French tended to be more pro-Serb than other countries. That's no secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. Now, if you go to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So were the Greeks, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So were the Greeks.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all right. And if you haven't gathered by my last name, I'm Greek.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I assume as much as well. Okay. If we could go to 296, which would have been the next page. 31 December 1992. Just very quickly. In the first paragraph. This is with respect to Susak. This is from David Owen to Cyrus Vance -- or from David Owen, copied to Cyrus Vance, and it says here that there was a conversation with Mr. Susak, and he says: "He told me that he met or spoke, I wasn't sure which, to Izetbegovic after we left on Wednesday, and Izetbegovic was mainly concerned about how he could sell to the Muslim population sharing provinces with Croats, and he suggested," he suggested, that is Susak suggested, "that Boban and Izetbegovic should go on a joint speaking tour explaining that there would be a total educational freedom for Muslim schools for Muslim classes within schools which is something that he had experienced in Canada." And it goes on a little bit more. Were you aware of this intervention or this conversation between Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would have read this memo, yes. It's copied to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it seems here that Susak is -- is recommending that Boban and Izetbegovic go together because Izetbegovic is having concerns about selling the programme to his own people.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say that -- that he did have a problem at times convincing his own people what he -- he was trying to achieve?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You'll recall that when the map was presented to the three warring parties at Geneva on January 2nd, we've already reviewed that, it was accepted by the Bosnian Croats and not accepted by the Bosnian Serbs or by the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to page 300. That's a couple of pages down, and I will be referencing on this page just so we know what we're looking at. At the very end of the page you'll say it says "Notes ICFY: Lord Owen's meeting with President Mitterrand - 14 January 1993. Also sent to Danish EC Presidency." Now, we're not going to read page 301. There's no need for that. The Court can read it at some point. But if we could go to the following page, page 302, paragraph 5, I thought that this may be of some interest. "Lord Owen informed Mitterrand that he and Vance intended to travel to Zagreb on 15 January to meet Izetbegovic and Boban with Tudjman. It was important to try to get a common --"

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. What page are you on? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 302. 302. It should be --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Thank you. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No problem. And it's paragraph number 5. You will see it --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm keep reading. It says: "It was important to get a common Muslim/Croat position on the map, and on an interim government. The need for this had become all the more urgent as a result of the increased tension and fighting between the Muslims and the Croats. Lord Owen asked Mitterrand to emphasise these issues during his meeting with Tudjman, which Mitterrand agreed to do so." Is that consistent with your memory, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we turned -- if we could turn to the next page. This would be 307. And now we've up to 29 January 1993. This is Lord Owen's personal telegram to Sir Robin Renwick. You must have known who Sir Robin Renwick is or was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I was but I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was the UK Ambassador to the United States, I believe. And we'll skip the first paragraph. The second paragraph we'll just look at very briefly. It says: "Even though Croatia has now moved to the top of the agenda, all of these issues are linked. We have to have a decentralised provincial government in Bosnia-Herzegovina to cope with the Serb and Croat special national needs: For exactly the same reason, Tudjman has to give special status, autonomy, to the Serbs in Croatia, and we must now for him to act." If we can pause there for a second. Obviously you know exactly what he's talking about, the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. They were not a constituent peoples. They were a national minority but they --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were always a constituent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- the concepts -- sorry, the woman nods but she's probably Croat. The concept of constituent people covered all of Yugoslavia. That's one of the reasons that Milosevic would be -- for example, when one would say to Milosevic about Kosovo, you know, you shouldn't lord it over the Muslims because the ethnic Albanian Muslims in Kosovo are 85, 90 per cent, and you're a minority. Would say, no, no, no, the Serbs can never be a minority. We are a constituent people, et cetera, et cetera, he went on. All the three sides were very conscious of their -- of -- I see one of -- there's a lot of heads shaking no, so perhaps they should speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, they don't need to speak because I can speak for them. I think that --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- under the contusion they did make a distinction between constituent peoples within the republics and a national minority, and as far as I understand, and we don't have to debate the point, but the Serbs in Croatia, even though there was a large number of them, were considered a national minority. Nonetheless very important, but somewhat different than a constituent peoples because obviously that was one of the reasons in Bosnia-Herzegovina the three constituent peoples were concerned and as a result had a whole war over it. Anyway, let's leave that aside. Let's move on to the next paragraph. Here he's talking about -- I'll just read part it of. He says: "As you will have gathered at the Prime Minister's seminar, I am, to put it mildly, not happy with thee administration's conduct." The administration he's talking about, probably the US administration?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is no question. He means the new Clinton administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they'd been in for seven days now?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, yeah, nine days, exactly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. "First we had Eagleburger, and that must have been Lawrence Eagleburger?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Demob," I don't know what that means, "happy grandstanding his way around Europe."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, "demob" stands for demobilisation and demob happy is a rather informal way of saying Eagleburger strongly supported demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Lord Owen believed and thought -- believed strongly that that was an unviable proposal so that he criticised Eagleburger for making it. And that's what he's doing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Eagleburger was, in all fairness to Eagleburger he had been an old Balkan hand himself. He had spent some time in Yugoslavia as an ambassador, I believe, at one point?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He was a former American Ambassador to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it goes on: "Now we have this administration briefing the press in a way that could not -- that could not but stiffen those Muslims who want to continue the war. We have Sacirbey telling everyone that the US administration has said that they should not feel any need to sign the map. We know that Tudjman had formal representations from the United States, or from the US against the Croats putting any pressure on the Muslims to sign up -- to sign up for our package. A continuation of these actions threatens to undermine our whole approach." And then it goes on to see: "See UKMIS Geneva Tel 84 and fax of document on interim agreements -- arrangements." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's park here. Sacirbey, you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe he's still in the US?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he's in gaol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he made bail. He's on provisional release pending extradition to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm pleased to hear that for his sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think it was a 1 million dollar bail, so obviously somebody came up with it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was for the benefit of the court, the Bosnian government ambassador to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, it seems to me that at this point in time, at least if we look into this, that this new administration is -- sort of is encouraging or is sort of giving the nod to the Muslims to sort of jettison or not go along with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan because perhaps the US administration has different -- has a different approach. Would that be a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at some point in fact Lord Owen describes a meeting between Mr. Vance and Warren Christopher, and as I understand Warren Christopher at one point worked for Mr. Vance when Mr. Vance was Secretary of State under the Carter administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Warren Christopher, Secretary Christopher, was Cyrus Vance's deputy when he was Secretary of State, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Vance's number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I was Vance's number two in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And at least the exchange, it would appear, we might get to something in here --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at that meeting. There were only four people. If you were interested, I can tell you about. There were only four people at the meeting, Vance, myself, Christopher, and an assistant named Johnson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right let me --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- tell the Court about that meeting if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We may get to that at some point, but needless to say, as I understand it, at least Mr. -- Lord Owen felt or believed that this administration was either misinformed or uninformed.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very good characterisation of Lord Owen's view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you share that view?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the US administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that time with respect to what was happening was misinformed or uninformed?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might not go as far as Lord Owen, but, yes, basically I share that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would also share his view that Mr. Vance was rather agitated, angry, maybe angry is too harsh of a word, but certainly irritated with the way the administration was treating him or behaving towards him?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Their treatment of him was -- he's a great figure. Their treatment of his was gracious and respectful at all times, but he naturally did not appreciate their less than whole hearted support of the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In all due -- in all fairness, at that point he's not working for the US administration. He's working for the UN?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we can even see that little cryptic note you make when Eagleburger tells you, you don't have to put down your pen. You're not with the Americans; right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Secretary Vance and I were representatives of the Secretary-General, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you certainly weren't carrying water for the State Department while you were working for the Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, that's what I wanted to make sure, that. And I have the highest respect for the late Cyrus Vance. He was a terrific, a terrific diplomat and lawyer. If we go on to the next paragraph, in the middle of it, it says -- maybe we could read the whole paragraph. "You are not -- you are free to say in whatever way you think best that if they do not extend to us even that courtesy that I will take up the cudgels in every form available to me, the secretary counsel, Congress --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "The Congress and every TV studio that asks me in. Incidentally, you can book me in for any interviews you think appropriate. I would expect to fly to the US on Monday and be there for at least a week. In short, they will not just be dealing with Vance on this issue, and I will not mince words. Nor will I hesitate if we are being belonged by Izetbegovic to reveal some of Ganic and Silajdzic's tactics - the latest example we have is of Muslim fighters firing mortars at Serbs from within the grounds of the main hospital in Sarajevo. The American public has been given a completely one-sided view of what is happening in the former Yugoslavia. I have not spent five months sweating my guts out for this settlement package to see it blocked by a new American Administration, particularly when all the signs are that it will have the support of the European Community and the Russian Federation. If the Administration has objections to our plan, then let them express them in the consultations that will have to take place around a Security Council Resolution." Now, let me go on to the next page. If we go towards the middle of the page, it would be the fourth paragraph, it starts with: "The Muslims also have a strategic agenda. The Serbs recently put down a suggestion for dealing with the eastern borders with Serbia effectively bisecting the whole eastern strip of Bosnia-Herzegovina, (see sketch map faxed through separately). Their suggested province 4 would be Muslim and province 6, Serb. Yet the Muslims turned this down, even though it is a far better ethnic balance. Why? Because they want Tuzla province, which they control, to cut the Serb horseshoe around their central areas, and they want to be able to control at least part of the border with Serbia themselves. It was because we knew that this was their strategic demand that we had to play around with the rather absurd enclave of Sekovici and the odd tail up from the Eastern Herzegovina province to include Rudo and Cajnice," sorry about the name, "which from the Serbs means they partially block the Bosnian Muslims from the Muslims in the Sandzak area." And then he goes on to says you noted here today at one point: "There are no innocents in this business, least of all the Muslims. The Muslims have been given the main industrial areas and most of the natural resources. We were amazed how foolishly the Serbs clung to their obsession with ethnic villages and virtually ignored industrial and economic factors." All right. From -- from here it would -- do you agree with Lord Owen when he's -- with what he's saying to the UK Ambassador, Sir Robin Renwick, on 29 January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I agree with what? You --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All of that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to go through it and I don't think we have time, but I will summarise for the sake of the Court very briefly. This 29 January was the very eve of our move of the conference from Geneva to New York, as I noted in my witness statement, we recommenced on 1 February. The early Clinton administration reaction was in the extreme pro-Muslim and that you see Lord Owen was objecting to that, and he cited as an example, a well-known example that we reported at the time, I did so myself, that some Muslims fired mortars at the Serb gunners in the hills around Sarajevo, and they fired them from the grounds of the main Sarajevo hospital knowing or knowing almost certainly that the Serbs would respond by attacking the mortars. Then they could call the international press and say, "See? The Serbs are bombing the hospital," which they did. So there were no angels, there were no innocents in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to what Lord Owen says, the Muslims also have a strategic agenda, he is of course correct. That's why the map was so argued, because all three sides, and I noted that in my witness statement, sought to gain advantages on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I just wanted to point that out, and the Judges will have the rest of the text and we will help them with what we believe what conclusion should be reached. If we could -- I'm running out of time, unfortunately, but if we could just go to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should say that when we got to America, Lord Owen was frequently on television and made these views known to -- to the public at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. If we could look at next just very quickly the following document, which is dated 1 February 1993, and that's on page 311. Just -- just very briefly, paragraph 1 it says: "Owen seriously dismayed by performance of Secretary Christopher." Were you there -- were you there when --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already reported to you that I was at the meeting on February 1 at the US mission to the United Nations between Christopher, Lord Owen, Secretary Vance, myself, and the note-taker Christopher had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I don't want to go into any more of that -- that into that document. I mean, I do, but I don't have the time. But if we go into the following document, that would be on page 312, 5 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I comment for the benefit of the Court, very briefly, on the meeting of February 1, since you've raised it twice?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead, sir, but --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead. I wish you had independent time for this but go ahead. No, no, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secretary Vance explained the plan. I have with me in my hotel room, whose speaking points that I drafted for him, and I would be happy to submit them to the Court that's what Secretary Vance said. Nobody has seen them but Secretary Vance and me. And I have brought hem with me if the Court would wish to see them, but I don't they add anything, frankly. Warren Christopher was not so much misinformed or ignorant as very strongly advocating the Muslim line, and at one point in the conversation, Lord Owen was talking about the JNA and the Bosnian Serb army, and he said and all he meant to say was that they were a uniformed military with a long history, the JNA, and -- and they were highly disciplined, and secretary Christopher took umbrage at that remark because -- and said something to the effect that, yes, highly disciplined for ethnic cleansing. He thought -- Christopher thought that Lord Owen was complimenting the Serb army, and of course he wasn't, but these are the kinds of things that happen when people who hold differing views speak across the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the main, I have to say, it was not a satisfactory meeting for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And I think there's some notes to that, but let's go to the next document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document which is on page 312. At the very last paragraph of this page, I'm going to just read in the middle of the paragraph it says: "It is astonishing how little the new administration has learned about Bosnia during the two and a half month transition." And I guess they're talking about this transitional period from winning the election to --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between -- from November to beginning of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this too much but if you go on to the next page, 313, very briefly because again I'm running out of time, it just says here on one, two, three -- the fourth paragraph, second sentence, it says here: "But it was important to recognise that the Bosnian government did not really exist as a functioning government. The Prime Minister, Akmadzic, would be in the Croat delegation. He would be able to testify that the Bosnian Presidency has never discussed who should lead the Bosnian delegation to the talks, nor what their negotiating position would be. Silajdzic would come to New York and say that the government was not prepared to negotiate unless arrangements were agreed first for the control of heavy weapons and a complete opening of -- opening up of humanitarian corridors. The government had first accepted the cessation of hostility -- hostilities paper, but then refused to sign it on the bogus pretext that Nambiar had made amendments that they needed time to consider." Nambiar, of course, is a general, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Satish Nambiar, an Indian general, was the principal military officer. He was in charge of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Then it goes on: "They were now demanding that there should be a National Army - a position which I had myself originally supported in Geneva but which all three factions had hereto refused to accept. None of these 'government"" positions had been discussed by the Bosnian Presidency. The minister of defence had not been consulted nor the leaders in Bihac and Tuzla." Now, do you share this observation by Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several times when the Bosnian government was obstructive, no question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it also seems to indicate that the so-called government is Alija Izetbegovic and maybe Silajdzic and Ganic, but he's not consulting the Presidency keeping in mind he that has one vote among all the others?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already stated and we've discussed and I so stated in paragraph 11 of my witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I said -- where I said that Izetbegovic and Silajdzic represented Muslim interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. All right. I have one last document. I have about an hour's worth of cross-examination on your notes, but I don't have the time. But if I could just go to the very last document, 1D 01316. And just so you know, I think I read parts of your diary six or seven times.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six or seven times?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2.000 pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not all of it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately. But I mean, I --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say, that's 14.000 pages. I commend you. My handwriting isn't that terrific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I went and I analysed it by chapters, but unfortunately we don't have time. But I will be pointing this out to the Chamber at some point?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I can provide any further assistance to you or to the Trial Chamber on the matter of my diaries, I'm not joking here, Mr. Karnavas, I'm at your disposal. So if there are any further questions. I have the originals, by the way, with me at my home in New York. I had given them to the Trial Chamber and they were here for a couple of years and that's why you have the copies, but the Tribunal returned them to me, but if you ever wanted to see the originals, I would make them available to you, Mr. President. I'm not suggesting you need to see them, but if the question arose as to their authenticity or whether there were later changes made, and there were none, but I would be happy to cooperate with the -- with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we're not suggesting any changes were being made, just so you know, but I just found there were some interesting aspects in your diary which unfortunately I would need an hour or so to discuss with you. But if we could look at this last document, 1D 01316.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I pulled this off the internet.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is or is not authentic, and that's why I'm putting it to you. It looks like an interview that claims you had in April 15, 2006.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite familiar with it. It is authentic. Some of the translation is a bit shaky, but it's authentic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you did in fact have this interview in -- in your comments regarding Tudjman, for instance, you say at the bottom of the page, for instance, the page -- the first page, it says: "I can say openly that I liked Tudjman because he was a serious politician who kept his word. True, he had a rigid style of behaviour which many falsely interpreted, especially Western journalists, but all my experience with Tudjman are positive. After all, Tudjman, who led his country in war, with an imposed arms embargo, could not act like Gandhi. He was cooperative, wanted peace, and actively participated in negotiations in The Hague, Geneva and Zagreb. They resented that he changed street names from the communist times, and while he was doing that Milosevic was killing Croats in Eastern Slavonia." I won't go on because I think it's -- the document speaks for itself, but is that -- is that your recollection of how you describe Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly how I described him. It's a direct quote. And when I'm talking about the desire for peace, I'm talking specifically about the fighting in Croatia. You can see I talk about The Hague, the conference in The Hague. There was never a conference in The Hague about Bosnia, so I'm talking here about Bosnia. And the changing of the street names was Croatia, so this is directed -- and Eastern Slavonia is Croatia, so I'm talking here about the Serb attack on Croatia and President Tudjman's response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So I take it we -- did you want to make any particular corrections to the text or do you stand by the text --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just what I've told you that where -- when I say, "Tudjman, who led his country in war," that's the fighting in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- "with an imposed arms embargo from 1991, Security Council Resolution 713," you may check that if you wish, Security Council Resolution 713, "with an imposed arms embargo could not act like Gandhi. He was cooperative, wanted peace, and actively participated." This is all concerning the Serb incursions, the Serb aggression in Croatia. This is not referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when I say they resented that he changed the street names, "they," of course, are the Serbs. So, yes, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But if we go into the next paragraph, and I just want to -- just want to read it to make sure that it also -- you stand by this one, this statement as well. It says: "I was with Tudjman -- I was with Tudjman when the exodus of Croatians from --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "Ilok began. He said to me Mr. Ambassador do something. It is terrible what my people are experiencing. Then Vance called Milosevic but he answered that he does not know what he's talking that he has nothing to do with Ilok. That man never spoke the truth. Tudjman was intelligent. He knew history, and speaking openly with his leadership Croatians through Operation Storm and other military actions saved Bosnia-Herzegovina. At a meeting in Sarajevo in 1991, Izetbegovic told me that he will demand of the JNA to leave BiH, and I asked him: 'Where is your army? Who will defend you if the JNA does not comply?' I quickly realised that in Bosnia only the Croats offered organised defence and saved it from downfall, something often kept quietly by the media as well as politicians." Now, earlier you indicated that you stood by your interview. I take it you stand by this -- this paragraph as well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I apologise for the pace. I apologise if I was disputatious or even rude at times, but it was not my intention, sir. Thank you for coming to The Hague to give your testimony, and I thank you on behalf of Dr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I thank a you. You were entirely gracious and at no time did I feel that you were speaking rudely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is quarter past 5.00. Maybe this a good moment to take our next break in order to allow for the next Defence team to prepare themselves. Who will be the next? Mr. Praljak, you? Very well. It is quarter past 5.00, and we're going to take a 20-minute break, everybody. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now resume, and before I give the floor to Mr. Praljak, the Chamber has deliberated, on we would like to inform you of the time that the two parties have spent so far. Mr. Karnavas has used three hours and 25 minutes -- 28 minutes, almost three hours. Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Praljak, how much time would you need? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I have my time, which is one hour and 20 minutes, and half of Mr. Pusic's time, and I will see how far that will get me, and maybe later Mrs. Alaburic will also want to give me some of her time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We plan to use our own one hour and 20 minutes that we have been allocated for our cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are planning to use our own time unless we reach an agreement with General Praljak on giving him some of our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you have not informed me exactly. Ms. Alaburic, approximately how much time, how many minutes, how many hours, weeks, I don't know. Give us an estimate of the time that you might need.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that for this calculation the best thing would be for you to calculate that I will use my time, an hour and 20 minutes, in case Mr. Praljak will need some time, we will give him some time, but the total time will be the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] We have given our time to the Defence of Dr. Prlic, and we will not have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, according to our previous agreement, we have also given our time to be shared between Mr. Prlic and General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have to take into account two factors for tomorrow. First of all, there might be some questions from the Judges, additional re-examination by the Prosecution, and we also have to dedicate time to Mr. Prlic and the others who will wish to intervene on the issues of the procedure. Very well, then. Mr. Praljak, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you may begin. Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobra Dan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At the beginning of my cross-examination, I would like to agree a certain procedure. Actually, I have a request upon you given the little time that I have. You are a very experienced diplomat. You're a professor. You will have a lot to tell us about what happened in the former Yugoslavia. Unfortunately, I have worded my questions based on some data, some facts and documents, but I would kindly ask you to answer my questions as precisely as possible by using the words to the effect, "Yes, I know," or, "I don't know." And then when I put to you some conclusions or a thesis that will arise from that you will be kindly asked to say, "I agree," or "I don't agree with your thesis." I'm asking you this only because of the time limitations. I would very gladly listen to all your explanations but I don't have the time. So I kindly ask you to cooperate and I thank you in advance for that. Can we have on e-court 3D 00871, please. While this is done -- while this is being done, Ambassador, you've been looking at the map which is next to you. On that map there are two things that I am interested in and that I'm going to be asking you about. Do you know that from the beginning of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina a certain number of HVO brigades were under the command of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being aware of that fact. I just don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you cannot either confirm or deny the fact that is depicted on the map, and that is that towards the end of 1992, when Vance-Owen Plan was completed, 11 brigades of the HVO and a battalion in Bihac were under the command of the BiH army? You are not aware of that? You cannot confirm that because you are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I was aware that in the Bihac pocket, as it was called, Cazinska Krajina, called it the Bihac pocket, that the BiH army was in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Ambassador, please. Did you know that towards the end of 1992, 11 HVO brigades and an HVO battalion, which was in Bihac, were all under the command of the BiH army? Did you know it or did you not know that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I knew that. I'm not sure, but, you know, it was 15 years ago, but I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the map, you will see some of the axes of attack by the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska, which took place during the conflict with the HVO after something that is known as the agreement in Graz between Boban and Karadzic. According to some statements, an agreement was signed there between Croats and Serbs. On this map you can see what happened after that date. One of the things was an attack by the JNA from Livno to Split, also Jajce, also Posavina. Sir, you're looking at the wrong map. Not the one on e-court. Not the one on the screen but the big map next to you. In other words, after the so-called agreement that I have just mentioned, there were major fights in the Neretva valley between the Croatian Defence Council and the JNA. The JNA wanted to break through to Split via Livno. They attacked Jajce in order to cut Bosnia and Herzegovina in half. They proceeded along the Lasva Valley towards Sarajevo, and there were also major attacks on Posavina in order to expand the Serb corridor. Were you aware of those conflicts between the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska on the one side and the HVO on the other side, which took place after something that Boban allegedly signed in Graz together with Karadzic? Did you know or did you not know? Please answer that, and then we will proceed after your answer.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew of the -- of the JNA and VRS attacks in the Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we now go back to the map which is now on e-court, on the screen, please? Do you know that in 1985 the JNA had the following deployment of corps and armies such as depicted on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with the JNA of deployment of 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the next page of the same document? The document with the same number but the next page, please. That's it. Do you know that in 1987 the JNA was reorganised and that it reorganised the territory of Yugoslavia, which was in keeping with the proclaimed political goals by the policies in Belgrade according to which everything that was east of the Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag line should be placed under Yugoslavia, and the assumption was that Slovenia would leave that state? In other words, that would mean the Greater Serbia. Are you familiar with this territorial organisation, and would you say that this corresponded with what you know -- what you knew at the time about the goals of the Serbian politics?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1987, General, I was not involved with Yugoslavia except that Yugoslavia was somewhere in that period a member of the Security Council, and I was an American Ambassador to the United Nations and represented my country on the Security Council. But these specific military dispositions were not brought to my attention in New York in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. I still would like you to answer as short as possible. Can we have the next page of this same document? The next page of the same document, please. I'm now going to ask you -- this is the document that I wanted. You were in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Is it true that at the request of the international community the Geneva agreement was signed on the 23rd of November, 1991? According to that agreement, Croatia lifted the blockade of all the barracks of the JNA in Croatia. Do you know that at the request of the international community, Croatia lifted blockade from the barracks, and it had already been under attack at the time? Are you aware of all that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in Geneva with Secretary Vance and Lord Carrington and November 23rd, 1991, when in the Palais des Nations that agreement was signed between the Croatians and the Serbs and the agreement was that they, Croatian government, would lift the blockade of the JNA barracks. They had them all over the country. And the hope was that the blockades wrote be lifted by the end of the year, and indeed it happened at the very end of the year. The last blockade that was lifted was actually at the aircraft repair facility at the Zagreb airport, which you're undoubtedly familiar with. And since the blockade was lifted, we gathered a few days later, January 2, 1992, and that agreement was signed between Defence Minister Gojko Susak and a JNA general establishing a complete cessation of hostilities in Croatia, and the agreement stayed in force and that's the origin --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please. I apologise, sir. I apologise once again. At the beginning we said that you know a lot and that to my one question you could provide us with a lot of information over the next hour. However, I kindly ask you, Ambassador, if my question is, "Are you aware of an agreement?", I would be quite happy if your answer was, "Yes, I do," or, "No, I don't," so I could move on. I would very much like to spend five days talking to you, but I don't have the time. Is it true that the forces that left Croatia according to that agreement went to Bosnia and Herzegovina and were deployed in the way depicted in the map that you have in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean JNA forces or Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: JNA forces. There were no Croatian forces at the time. JNA forces that left Croatia ended up being deployed in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is depicted in the map. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware of the redeployment of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If these are the starting points, would you then agree that the Geneva agreement allowed for the deployment of the JNA from the barracks in Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina and that this contributed to the peace in that republic in the best possible way? And I repeat my question. Would you agree that the Geneva agreement was a real, true contribution to the peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina? In other words, whether the deployment of these forces was really beneficial for the peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It made no difference. No, I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Can we now move on and show the next map. Please skip the next one, actually, and display the map that shows the aggression against Croatia that originated from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ambassador, on this map you will see how Bosnia and Herzegovina had become the main polygon for the attack on continuation of aggression against the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will remind you of Dubrovnik, Ploce, Split, Zadar, Sibenik, Sisak, Slavonski Brod, and partly the territory towards Eastern Slavonia, i.e., towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events you're talking about took place between June 1991 and January 2, 1992. That's the period we're talking about, because they stopped with the agreement reached, as I mentioned, on 2 January between the Croatian government and the JNA, and the JNA was required by that agreement to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- withdraw its forces from the Republic of Croatia, which it did eventually but not immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of transformation of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina took place into the army of Republika Srpska, and do you know how many attacks were mounted after the reaching of the agreement against Slavonski Brod and other towns in Croatia despite the cease-fire achieved? Were you aware of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina continued serving not only as the place where Posavina Serbs were trying to gain ground but also as the area from where attacks were launched into Croatia on the town such as Slavonski Brod, Sisak, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ECMM monitors did not report such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, was he able in any way to prevent the Yugoslav People's Army and the army of the Republika Srpska to use the BiH as the basis from where they were launching their aggression on Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have physical control of most of the country, so he could not prevent the JNA, which later, as you know, General, and as you were leading me to say, became --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the VRS. Yes, you're quite right that he would not have had the capacity to stop the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Is it logical that the president, Tudjman, should be interested in the military and political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in view of all these events and that he should be playing an active role in the entire game? Is it only logical on the basis of the military and political developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you heard, Mr. Karnavas and I discussed that at length. Yes, he was interested, and it was logical that he should be interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 3D 00869. 3D 00869. Ambassador, are you aware of the fact that in 1988 the Yugoslav Presidency, together with the army and the police, mounted a police and military coup in Kosovo imprisoning thousands of Kosovo Albanians in the process? Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The world press covered the fighting and the attacks, mutual attacks in Kosovo. The ethnic Albanians went after the Serb. The Serbs went after the Albanians. And, of course, in 1989 Mr. Milosevic made his very important speech about those attacks and the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have the next map in the same bundle. There, Ambassador, you will be able to see Yugoslavia and the two autonomous provinces that were the component parts of the Yugoslav federation, namely Kosovo and Vojvodina. This is my question: Are you aware that by a unilateral act of the Serbian leadership led by Slobodan Milosevic the autonomy of Vojvodina and Kosovo was abolished, which meant that the constitution of the SFRY had been infringed? It was in that same year after Gazimestan. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 3D 00870, please. 3D 00870. This map dated 17 August 1990, on that particular date the helicopters of the Croatian ministry of the interior headed towards Knin together with the police forces in an attempt to lift the blockade of the roads that had been blocked. Are you aware of the fact that these helicopters were prevented from carrying out their duties pursuant -- or, rather, by the JNA, which sent out aircraft to intercept these helicopters on the 17th of August, 1990, requesting that they return back to Zagreb, thus siding with the rebels and aiding to the infringement and dissolution of the Croatian constitution?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved with Yugoslavia in 1990. As I've reported to the Court, Mr. Vance and I became involved at the beginning of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, were you aware from any sources that the JNA had more than 2.000 tanks, several hundred aircraft, more than 10.000 artillery pieces, two destroyers, more than 100 combat helicopters, and so on and so forth? Were you aware of the fact that it was a very powerful military force?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The international institute of strategic studies published annually - it still does - what they call the Military Balance, and in that publication they give the facts and figures for all the world's major armies, and the JNA, which then was the Yugoslav national army, was covered. I'm trying to answer your question, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 3D 00872, please. 3D 00872. All of this is leading to a logical inference. Am I right in saying that the Yugoslav People's Army, as powerful as it have, collected all of its -- all of the weaponry of the Territorial Defence both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina before launching an aggression against these two countries? Were you aware of the fact that the Territorial Defence forces in the republics had their own weapons that had been purchased from the funds from within the republic and that all of that weaponry had been forcibly seized by the Yugoslav People's Army in the wake of the aggression?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware that the JNA, either subvert the Territorial Defence units under their control or gave weapons to the Serbs to work in conjunction with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to read an excerpt from an interview of yours where you say: "My experience told me that this wasn't true, rather, that it's not true what the ordinary people thought, that there was not going to be any war, and that a war will most certainly break out because I distrusted Milosevic."
